catalog_quote: Due to the preliminary nature of our data we do not yet have a complete picture of stress in Kui. Nonetheless, preliminary conclusions may be drawn: stress appears to be based on moraic trochees that are right aligned. However, even these preliminary trends have exceptions in our small dataset. Table 4 gives a sample of the possibilities. In disyllabic words the weight of the final syllable is significant. Final heavy syllables attract stress: heavy syllables may be defined by the presence of long vowels, diphthongs or a coda. In other disyllables stress falls on the first syllable. This suggests a trochaic structure sensitive that is to syllable weight. These two groups can be seen in (15). However, there are exceptions, given in (16), which create stress differentiated minimal pairs with regularly stressed items. These are both somewhat exceptional items in other ways: /u'ti/ is vulgar while /i'ka/ is a specifically vocative form (cf: the regular form /-nana/ 'older sibling'). (15) ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is assigned by a right-aligned moraic trochee: it falls on the final syllable when that syllable is heavy (bimoraic) and otherwise on the penultimate syllable; the authors present this as a preliminary tendency with exceptions.

new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in the authors' small Kui dataset; the snippet is cut on both sides, so the preceding hedge ('.. stress in Kui') and the examples in Table 4 are not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Windschuttel & Shiohara 2017 describe Kui proper (Masin-lak) of south-west Alor (Lerabaing/Buraga/Moru), i.e. kuii1253 itself; the closely related Kiraman(g) variety (Stokhof's list 24, treated by some as a dialect) is not covered by the quoted statement.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement (right-aligned moraic trochee = weight-sensitive) and adds the weight definition (long vowel, diphthong or coda), the default initial stress in light disyllables, and the two lexical exceptions /u'ti/ and /i'ka/. Google's tokenised spacing before punctuation was normalised in the quote; no words were changed or supplied, and adjacent snippets overlap by several words. Cross-reference held by the project: Schapper 2020 (TAP vol. 3, p. 263) lists Kui (Windschuttel and Shiohara 2017: 118-119) among Alor-Pantar languages whose trochaic system 'may be disrupted by heavy syllables occurring in non-penultimate position', which is compatible.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-aligned moraic trochee: in a disyllable, a heavy final syllable (long vowel, diphthong or coda) takes the stress; otherwise stress falls on the first syllable. Longer words are not described in the snippets (Table 4 and examples (15)-(16) were not retrievable). The authors call the analysis preliminary and based on a small dataset.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any retrieved snippet.
new_statements.exceptions: 'However, there are exceptions, given in (16), which create stress differentiated minimal pairs with regularly stressed items. These are both somewhat exceptional items in other ways: /u'ti/ is vulgar while /i'ka/ is a specifically vocative form (cf: the regular form /-nana/ 'older sibling').' (p. 118) -- i.e. two lexically final-stressed light disyllables forming minimal pairs with regularly (initially) stressed items.
new_statements.identity_note: Windschuttel & Shiohara 2017 describe Kui of south-west Alor (Glottolog kuii1253; LexiRumah 'Kui, Labaing'); the Google Books hits for 'Kui' in HuoiAQAAMAAJ ('Stress in Kui is manifested as increased syllable duration (Winfield 1928)') concern the Dravidian Kui of India, not this language, and were disregarded.
